Issued at 134 AM MDT Tue Sep 1 2026

This morning we say goodbye to meteorological summer for another 
year. And we enter what is the favorite month for many Wyoming 
residents, September. The number of tourists drops substantially, 
especially after Labor Day, so we have the state more to ourselves. 
It is usually a fairly dry month (with some exceptions). And 
temperatures are usually pretty nice, with comfortably warm days and 
cool nights. However, I have witnessed a few snowstorms in 
September in my almost 15 years at the office. But, none of 
those on the horizon, at least for the next week.

We are seeing some needed moisture this morning, in the form of a 
plume of monsoonal moisture and a shortwave lifting northward across 
the area. We do have some showers across the area this morning but 
as of right now, the heaviest showers are across Idaho. Most 
guidance does shift this eastward toward dawn and into the morning, 
with decent model agreement showing northwestern Wyoming seeing the 
steadiest and heaviest showers. Ensemble guidance is giving at least 
a 1 in 2 chance of a quarter of an inch of rain from through 
midnight tonight across the Tetons, Wind River Range and northern 
Salt and Wyoming Range, with the adjacent valleys having a 4 in 5 
chance of at least a tenth of an inch of rain. The chance of an inch 
or rain is small though, generally less than 1 out 3 and this is 
only at the highest elevations. As for flooding potential, it looks 
small at this point given that there is steering flow with these 
showers, so they should not be stationary. Precipitable water is 
also coming in about 15 to 20 percent less than yesterday, generally 
running 125 to 150 percent of normal versus 150 to 175 percent 
yesterday. The chance is not zero though. The best chance this 
morning would be in areas prone to southerly upslope, like the 
western Wind River Range. The chance is small though, generally less 
than 1 out of 5. There look to be two periods of showers. The 
initial one this morning with the wave lifting northward. The second 
will be this afternoon, as a trailing shortwave moves into western 
Wyoming. Most of this wave would remain West of the Divide, as 
downsloping west to southwesterly flow develops behind the wave. 
(Around a 1 in 4 chance west of the Divide, less than 1 out of 5 
East of the Divide except near the mountains). A few of these 
showers will linger into the evening and possibly after midnight 
before ending before dawn on Wednesday as drier air punches in from 
the south and west.

And now for something completely different, an 180 degree flip as it 
would be. Drier air will move across most of the area, with 
precipitable water values dropping back to close to normal values. 
We can't rule out a stray high based shower or thunderstorm but 
these would be few and far between (less than a 1 in 6 chance). For 
a few days, we will be shutting off the monsoon machine as it goes 
in for maintenance. However, we are in the process of changing the 
fluids in the famous Wyoming Wind Machine, which will be fired up 
for the first time in a while starting Wednesday. It will only be 
running at half power though, not red lining it Wyoming will be 
close to the middle point between and upper level low over the 
Pacific Northwest and a strong ridge over the southwest. The result 
will be a tight height gradient. We will also have around an 80 knot 
jet nearby. The result will be a breezy to windy afternoon across 
much of the area. With 700 millibar winds only expected to be around 
35 knots, high wind is not expected. Much of the area has at least a 
3 out of 5 chance of wind gusts over 30 mph. There is at least a 1 
in 2 chance of wind gusts past 40 mph in the favored southwest flow 
locations from South Pass through southern Johnson County. And 
humidity will be lower. However, it does not look quite low enough 
for critical fire weather at this time. The most likely spot would 
be Wind River Basin to the eastern Bighorn Basin where there is 
around a 1 in 2 chance of humidity falling to under 15 percent. It 
may not be for three hours though. So, for now we will hold off on 
any Fire Weather Watches. We will let the day crew take another look 
as they can issue watches and we could upgrade tomorrow night if 
need be. And with the downsloping flow, it will get quite warm. The 
warmer spots like the Bighorn Basin have at least a 1 in 2 chance of 
high temperatures reaching 90. 

Thursday at this point looks like a dry day across the area, With 
the jet still nearby, it will still be breezy to windy. However, dew 
points will be around 5 to 10 degrees lower. This will lead to a 
more widespread area of relative humidity under 15 percent. Wind may 
not be quite as strong, but there is still a greater than 1 out of 2 
chance of gusts over 25 much across much of the area. As a result,
